Primary batteries overview

Use once, then replace. Useful where storage life and convenience matter more than recharging.

Basic principlesTypes & featuresUnderstanding namesSelection criteria

What is a primary battery?

A primary battery converts the chemical energy of stored reactants into electricity. Typical products are not designed for recharging and are unsuitable for repeatedly reversing the used reactants electrically.

Chemical reactionElectrodes release or accept electrons
Powering a loadElectrons pass through the external circuit
ReplacementReplace the cell when reactants are depleted

The electrolyte carries ions; electrons flow through the external circuit connected to the device. Electrode–electrolyte combinations determine voltage, current capability, shelf life and cost.

Representative types and features

TypeChemistry & featuresTypical applications
Zinc–carbon · Zn/CZinc and manganese dioxide with a chloride-based electrolyte. Low cost, but less suitable for sustained high currents.Clocks and low-power remotes
Alkaline · Zn/MnO₂Zinc–manganese dioxide electrodes with an alkaline electrolyte. Usually better usable capacity and current capability than zinc–carbon cells.Everyday devices, toys and flashlights
Primary lithium batteriesMetallic lithium anodes. Cathodes distinguish lithium–manganese dioxide, lithium–thionyl chloride and other types. High energy density and long shelf life.Coin cells, meters and sensors
Silver oxide · Ag₂O/ZnSilver oxide cathodes and zinc anodes. Compact with relatively stable voltage; affected by silver prices.Watches and small precision devices
Zinc–air · Zn-airZinc reacts with oxygen from the air. Opening the air holes activates the battery; after activation, life decreases even without use.Hearing aids

Chemistry names and sizes are separate classifications

Alkaline describes the electrolyte, silver oxide names the cathode material, and primary lithium usually refers to the metallic lithium anode. Primary battery names therefore do not follow a single classification rule.

AA, AAA and coin refer to size and shape. AA products include alkaline primary and nickel-metal hydride secondary batteries with different voltages and operating requirements. Primary lithium and lithium-ion secondary batteries must also be distinguished.

How should you choose?

First check the required voltage and size, then compare current demand, temperature range, storage period and replacement interval. For frequent use, consider rechargeable lifetime costs. Do not recharge ordinary primary cells; collect used batteries separately for recycling.
